**AND1**is a legendary American **basketball and streetwear brand** that brought the hoop world much much more than cool t-shirts and awesome shoes. AND1 was more of a **cultural phenomenon** that appeared in the 2000s to greatly influence the world of basketball, create streetball fashion, a specific style of play, and a culture.
Shop AND 1 Shoes
Netflix released a **documentary chronicling the rise and fall of the brand** which, for lovers of the brand, is a trip down memory lane well worth taking. For fans of Weartesters, keep your eyes peeled for a cameo by your favorite internet sneaker guy. We will leave an image here so you can look for the exact moment. It is a small moment but is crazy to see how far Weartesters has come.

#### Latest AND1 performance model: AND1 Attack 3.0
Video 7

#### AND1 Basketball


## **AND1: Origins**
AND1 **began its journey in 1993** when Jay Coen Gilbert, Seth Berger, and Tom Austin started a t-shirt company out of the trunk of a car **while studying at the University of Pennsylvania**. The t-shirts featured the legendary faceless hooper and different trash talk phrases typically heard on the blacktops across America. The shirts were such a hit that they were snatched up by Foot Locker. **Within two years of its launch, AND1 products were available in 1,500 stores across the US.**

> A post shared by And1 – Australia + NZ (@and1_australia_nz)
> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by Tags & Threads (@tagsandthreads)
Then in 1996, Starbury himself, Coney Island’s finest **Stephon Marbury**, became the brand’s **first signature athlete**. Marbury was one of a brash new generation of players that brought a fresh street basketball flavor into the NBA. With Marbury´s signature shoe, AND1 launched its first pair of basketball sneakers and dove head-first into the footwear category. More on that classic first shoe later.
> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by @onfootarchives
> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by oNLy CooL SHoeS (@sneakersrules)
In the mid-1990s, AND1 was chugging along as just another basketball brand. That is, until a fateful day in 1998.**A tape was delivered to AND1** containing blurry, homemade streetball footage by a high school basketball coach from Queens, New York. The tape featured a spectacular New York City point guard by the name of **Rafer Alston, aka Skip To My Lou**. Having an “aka” was about to get wildly popular. And the videotape would soon be known as the **“Skip Tape”**.
> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by RetroRoundball Until Rapture (@thisdayinhoops)
> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by THG (@thehoopgods)

## **AND1: Origins**
Early in 1999, after a failed traditional marketing campaign, AND1 decided to use the “Skip tape” as a marketing tool and reprinted **50,000 copies**. Over the next eight weeks, it was distributed to basketball camps, clinics, and record labels. The tape would become the first basketball mixtape, and quickly made Alston an underground celebrity.
In the **summer of 1999**, AND1 created a clever marketing strategy that would prove pivotal to the brand. A free highlight tape was given to everyone who purchased AND1 products. The tape was known **as the AND1 Mixtape**. Approximately **200,000 tapes were distributed in three weeks**, making this promotion one of the most successful in U.S. retail history.
The **effects of this tape were felt in the NBA** and in the basketball world for over a decade as a generation of players copied and introduced this new school of streetball into the zeitgeist. Dunks and handles became “a must” in the NBA, while FG% and threes were an afterthought. Think of Jamal Crawford, Allen Iverson, Jason “White Chocolate” Williams, T-Mac, KG, Paul Pierce, Marbury, and Larry Hughes, just to name a few.
> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by NEVER NOT BALLIN‘ (@kickz93)
> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by Distant Replay (@distant_replay)
Even though AND1 had Starbury on the roster, they began to recruit more and more NBA players to wear their products – a major power play to compete with bigger brands such as Nike and adidas. Players like**Latrell Sprewell, Kevin Garnett, Larry Hughes and Jamal Crawford** brought AND1 into the national spotlight. The AND1 logo became one of the most common tattoos in the NBA, as clearly seen below:
> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by NBA THROWBACK (@notorious_big_bad_boy_)
> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by Larry Hughes Sr (@thereallhughes)

## **AND1: Origins**
During the 2000 All Star weekend, the brand’s most iconic shoe was featured prominently during the best dunk contest in the history of the NBA. Vince Carter strapped on a pair of the classic red and white AND1 Tai Chi and put on the greatest show the dunk contest has ever witnessed. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-OJMLCF5oK4&ab_channel=ESPN
As the 2001 season rolled around, AND1 was closing in on Nike. In only eight years, they had become the **second-largest basketball brand in the United States.**
The **AND1 Mixtape** became a cultural phenomenon. **Many streetball players reached legendary status**. They were known around the world exclusively by their nicknames: Hot Sauce, Half Man Half Amazing, AO, Black Widow, the Professor, Escalade, Alimoe, Spyda, The Air Up There, Skip to My Lou, and Main Event. If you lived through that era and didn’t try that Hot Sauce move with the spin and tucking the ball under your shirt, we can’t be friends. Just sayin’.
The soundtracks to the mixtapes were incredible, featuring artists like Snoop Dog, Mobb Deep, CNN, MOP, Method Man, GZA, Common, Talib Kwali, and more.
AND1 also created a world streetball tour, which was sort of like a hip-hop Harlem Globetrotters. They then added a reality TV show and even **released a video game**. The success of AND1 had the basketball shoe market on their heels scrambling to ride the streetball wave.
**EA Sports released the NBA and NFL street video games** series (some of the most fun games ever made, in my opinion). Nike put out their battleground product line and video series, while the NBA released the NBA street, ankle breakers, and dunk DVD series. The born-to-ball DVD was even a thing. It wasn’t the best era for technical basketball, but damn, it was fun.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GI4ilfUnNsw&ab_channel=RyanVanDusen
With our hearts filled with nostalgia, we present our top ten list of AND1 basketball shoes.

## **AND1’s Best Basketball Shoes**
### AND1 Marbury / Coney Island Classic
The shoe is legendary. It’s one of the most iconic silhouettes of the late 90s. Known today as the **AND1 Coney Island Classic**, these shoes were designed with streetball in mind. They were never a top-of-the-line performer by any stretch of the imagination, but they were an excellent incarnation of the street basketball subculture that took the NBA by storm.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1vC7pg7ltqk&feature=youtu.be&ab_channel=WearTesters
Stephon Marbury was the perfect player to rock AND1’s first basketball shoe. Marbury was a streetball legend from Coney Island, Brooklyn. Starbury was the prototypical New York point guard: flashy, stylish and could score with the best of them. The shoe prominently features the legendary AND1 logo and was built to withstand the rigors of outdoor play.

Picture this: it's 1996. Manila folders are still cool, nobody has a phone in their pocket, and a single chicken bucket has the power to unite an entire nation. Okay, maybe that's a stretch. But damn, the 1990s gave us some absolutely bonkers brand promotions that still make marketing professors weep with joy.
The nineties were the wild west of retail advertising. Brands weren't just selling products — they were launching full-blown cultural events that left everyone wondering, **"How did nobody think of this sooner?"** If you thought hashtags and viral TikToks invented hype, buckle up. Your grandparents already figured this out using turf voodoo dolls.

## KFC and Super Bowl VII — The Original Mother of All Campaigns
The most ridiculously successful 1990s brand promotion arguably came from KFC in 1991 — when they teamed up with the Super Bowl VII halftime show to announce free chicken to anyone wearing a bucket-striped outfit. Not kidding. The catch was the campaign was quietly used to legally reshape KFC's iconic red-and-white stripe logo. The FTC had basically said, "Your stripes look too close to the American flag. Fix it. Now." So KFC did the funniest logo pivot in retail history while still legal.

## KFC and Super Bowl VII — The Original Mother of All Campaigns

During Super Bowl VII's broadcast, they ran a widely discussed print and TV push bragging about **free red-and-white striped T-shirts**. The shirts came alongside their bucket-shaped logo refresh. It's almost like the United States government handed retail marketers a brand makeover for free. That sounds impossible, but here's the kicker: the _real_ megamarketing winner of the 1990s came later that very decade.

## KFC and Super Bowl VII — The Original Mother of All Campaigns
### Coolhaus Chicken Buckets — Er, Make That BE Mighty
By 1998, KFC orchestrated their **Be Mighty** Super Bowl campaign with a bucket-shaped parachute stunt over their flagship New York City location. Not kidding. A literal chicken bucket flew over Manhattan dressed as a World War II bomber. The stunt generated free press and traffic that took a small country's GDP to match. Marketing people still talk about it like it's the moon landing of promo stunts.
_RETRO 1990's Commercial Compilation Vol. 5: One hour of 1990's_
The timing was perfect too. The NBA Finals and Super Bowl crowd overlapped embarrassingly well. _People who'd never bought chicken before_ suddenly felt patriotic about dining on something deep-fried. That's successful brand promotion for you — making folks associate a juicy drumstick with the American flag itself.

## Other 1990s Legends That Refused to Sit Quietly
KFC wasn't alone in this chaos. The 1990s handed us the **Virgin Megastore launch**, whose opening-night pirate flag monument went viral in the pre-internet viral sense. Then there was **Walmart's Supercenter expansion**, which forced rural America to rethink "convenient shopping" around an 80,000-square-foot building shaped like a tumbleweed. In 1994, **Starbucks** also threw the first branded $6 latte, earning both people's affection and a lawsuit from angry commuters.
_The best adverts of the 1990s | Creative Bloq_
Not to be left out, **Toys "R" Us** opened Times Square in 2001 just weeks before igniting the best hype ticker I've ever seen — a giant statue giraffe inside stands taller than the Statue of Liberty. It was printed on every billboard within three miles. The promotion doubled foot traffic for three months straight, and the giraffe became the city's unofficial mascot for the next five years.

## Other 1990s Legends That Refused to Sit Quietly
### Why the 1990s Had No Rival
Here's the secret sauce: **decade-wide attention economies simply didn't exist yet**, so every creative stunt felt completely fresh. Brands could launch hyper-specific campaigns without a million other marketers screaming at the same consumer in the same fifteen seconds. There was room to be weird without drowning in competition. That's why nineties promotions have such lasting cult status among copywriters and creatives.
_1990s Commercial Compilation 📺 | Vintage TV Ads from the 90s - YouTube_
Subtle details mattered too. **Free samples**, tie-in merchandise, and physical stunts had outsized impact because everything felt tangible and freshly invented. There was no "keep scrolling" reflex blocking your message. Customers actually _engaged_ with a storefront banner like it was an invitation. That kind of trust is worth more than ten thousand paid impressions today.

## Unsurprising Yet Criminally Underrated: The 1990s Blueprint
Modern marketers steal from this era constantly, but rarely admit it. The nineties principles are dead simple: **make Americans feel something as they open their wallet**. Whether it was flag-paint-level patriotism or a $1 Happy Meal, the trick relied on emotional currency more than ad spend. That's a lesson most 2020s CMOs still absurdly overlook while chasing algorithm metrics.
So next time you skip a banner ad, remember: in 1996, a guy with a chicken bucket dressed as Uncle Sam got an _entire nation_ saluting. Those promotions looked crude by today's standards, yet they permanently reshaped how American households thought about brand identity. The 1990s didn't need a viral video — they needed a few buckets, a parade float, and sheer midsummer wanderlust. Mission accomplished, decades ago.

**AND1**is a legendary American **basketball and streetwear brand** that brought the hoop world much much more than cool t-shirts and awesome shoes. AND1 was more of a **cultural phenomenon** that appeared in the 2000s to greatly influence the world of basketball, create streetball fashion, a specific style of play, and a culture.
Shop AND 1 Shoes
Netflix released a **documentary chronicling the rise and fall of the brand** which, for lovers of the brand, is a trip down memory lane well worth taking. For fans of Weartesters, keep your eyes peeled for a cameo by your favorite internet sneaker guy. We will leave an image here so you can look for the exact moment. It is a small moment but is crazy to see how far Weartesters has come.

## **AND1: Origins**
AND1 **began its journey in 1993** when Jay Coen Gilbert, Seth Berger, and Tom Austin started a t-shirt company out of the trunk of a car **while studying at the University of Pennsylvania**. The t-shirts featured the legendary faceless hooper and different trash talk phrases typically heard on the blacktops across America. The shirts were such a hit that they were snatched up by Foot Locker. **Within two years of its launch, AND1 products were available in 1,500 stores across the US.**

> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by Tags & Threads (@tagsandthreads)
Then in 1996, Starbury himself, Coney Island’s finest **Stephon Marbury**, became the brand’s **first signature athlete**. Marbury was one of a brash new generation of players that brought a fresh street basketball flavor into the NBA. With Marbury´s signature shoe, AND1 launched its first pair of basketball sneakers and dove head-first into the footwear category. More on that classic first shoe later.
> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by @onfootarchives
> View this post on Instagram  
> A post shared by oNLy CooL SHoeS (@sneakersrules)
In the mid-1990s, AND1 was chugging along as just another basketball brand. That is, until a fateful day in 1998.**A tape was delivered to AND1** containing blurry, homemade streetball footage by a high school basketball coach from Queens, New York. The tape featured a spectacular New York City point guard by the name of **Rafer Alston, aka Skip To My Lou**. Having an “aka” was about to get wildly popular. And the videotape would soon be known as the **“Skip Tape”**.

## **AND1: Origins**
Early in 1999, after a failed traditional marketing campaign, AND1 decided to use the “Skip tape” as a marketing tool and reprinted **50,000 copies**. Over the next eight weeks, it was distributed to basketball camps, clinics, and record labels. The tape would become the first basketball mixtape, and quickly made Alston an underground celebrity.
In the **summer of 1999**, AND1 created a clever marketing strategy that would prove pivotal to the brand. A free highlight tape was given to everyone who purchased AND1 products. The tape was known **as the AND1 Mixtape**. Approximately **200,000 tapes were distributed in three weeks**, making this promotion one of the most successful in U.S. retail history.
The **effects of this tape were felt in the NBA** and in the basketball world for over a decade as a generation of players copied and introduced this new school of streetball into the zeitgeist. Dunks and handles became “a must” in the NBA, while FG% and threes were an afterthought. Think of Jamal Crawford, Allen Iverson, Jason “White Chocolate” Williams, T-Mac, KG, Paul Pierce, Marbury, and Larry Hughes, just to name a few.

Players like**Latrell Sprewell, Kevin Garnett, Larry Hughes and Jamal Crawford** brought AND1 into the national spotlight. ## **AND1: Origins**
During the 2000 All Star weekend, the brand’s most iconic shoe was featured prominently during the best dunk contest in the history of the NBA. Vince Carter strapped on a pair of the classic red and white AND1 Tai Chi and put on the greatest show the dunk contest has ever witnessed. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-OJMLCF5oK4&ab_channel=ESPN
As the 2001 season rolled around, AND1 was closing in on Nike. In only eight years, they had become the **second-largest basketball brand in the United States.**
The **AND1 Mixtape** became a cultural phenomenon. **Many streetball players reached legendary status**. They were known around the world exclusively by their nicknames: Hot Sauce, Half Man Half Amazing, AO, Black Widow, the Professor, Escalade, Alimoe, Spyda, The Air Up There, Skip to My Lou, and Main Event. If you lived through that era and didn’t try that Hot Sauce move with the spin and tucking the ball under your shirt, we can’t be friends. Just sayin’.
The soundtracks to the mixtapes were incredible, featuring artists like Snoop Dog, Mobb Deep, CNN, MOP, Method Man, GZA, Common, Talib Kwali, and more.
AND1 also created a world streetball tour, which was sort of like a hip-hop Harlem Globetrotters. They then added a reality TV show and even **released a video game**. The success of AND1 had the basketball shoe market on their heels scrambling to ride the streetball wave.
**EA Sports released the NBA and NFL street video games** series (some of the most fun games ever made, in my opinion). Nike put out their battleground product line and video series, while the NBA released the NBA street, ankle breakers, and dunk DVD series. The born-to-ball DVD was even a thing. It wasn’t the best era for technical basketball, but damn, it was fun.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GI4ilfUnNsw&ab_channel=RyanVanDusen

Picture this: it's 1996. Manila folders are still cool, nobody has a phone in their pocket, and a single chicken bucket has the power to unite an entire nation. Okay, maybe that's a stretch. But damn, the 1990s gave us some absolutely bonkers brand promotions that still make marketing professors weep with joy.
The nineties were the wild west of retail advertising. Brands weren't just selling products — they were launching full-blown cultural events that left everyone wondering, **"How did nobody think of this sooner?"** If you thought hashtags and viral TikToks invented hype, buckle up. Your grandparents already figured this out using turf voodoo dolls.
texts.1:
## KFC and Super Bowl VII — The Original Mother of All Campaigns
The most ridiculously successful 1990s brand promotion arguably came from KFC in 1991 — when they teamed up with the Super Bowl VII halftime show to announce free chicken to anyone wearing a bucket-striped outfit. Not kidding. The catch was the campaign was quietly used to legally reshape KFC's iconic red-and-white stripe logo. The FTC had basically said, "Your stripes look too close to the American flag. Fix it. Now." So KFC did the funniest logo pivot in retail history while still legal.

During Super Bowl VII's broadcast, they ran a widely discussed print and TV push bragging about **free red-and-white striped T-shirts**. The shirts came alongside their bucket-shaped logo refresh. It's almost like the United States government handed retail marketers a brand makeover for free. That sounds impossible, but here's the kicker: the _real_ megamarketing winner of the 1990s came later that very decade.
texts.3:
## KFC and Super Bowl VII — The Original Mother of All Campaigns
### Coolhaus Chicken Buckets — Er, Make That BE Mighty
By 1998, KFC orchestrated their **Be Mighty** Super Bowl campaign with a bucket-shaped parachute stunt over their flagship New York City location. Not kidding. A literal chicken bucket flew over Manhattan dressed as a World War II bomber. The stunt generated free press and traffic that took a small country's GDP to match. Marketing people still talk about it like it's the moon landing of promo stunts.
_RETRO 1990's Commercial Compilation Vol. 5: One hour of 1990's_
The timing was perfect too. The NBA Finals and Super Bowl crowd overlapped embarrassingly well. _People who'd never bought chicken before_ suddenly felt patriotic about dining on something deep-fried. That's successful brand promotion for you — making folks associate a juicy drumstick with the American flag itself.
texts.4:
## Other 1990s Legends That Refused to Sit Quietly
KFC wasn't alone in this chaos. The 1990s handed us the **Virgin Megastore launch**, whose opening-night pirate flag monument went viral in the pre-internet viral sense. Then there was **Walmart's Supercenter expansion**, which forced rural America to rethink "convenient shopping" around an 80,000-square-foot building shaped like a tumbleweed. In 1994, **Starbucks** also threw the first branded $6 latte, earning both people's affection and a lawsuit from angry commuters.
_The best adverts of the 1990s | Creative Bloq_
Not to be left out, **Toys "R" Us** opened Times Square in 2001 just weeks before igniting the best hype ticker I've ever seen — a giant statue giraffe inside stands taller than the Statue of Liberty. It was printed on every billboard within three miles. The promotion doubled foot traffic for three months straight, and the giraffe became the city's unofficial mascot for the next five years.
texts.5:
## Other 1990s Legends That Refused to Sit Quietly
### Why the 1990s Had No Rival
Here's the secret sauce: **decade-wide attention economies simply didn't exist yet**, so every creative stunt felt completely fresh. Brands could launch hyper-specific campaigns without a million other marketers screaming at the same consumer in the same fifteen seconds. There was room to be weird without drowning in competition. That's why nineties promotions have such lasting cult status among copywriters and creatives.
_1990s Commercial Compilation 📺 | Vintage TV Ads from the 90s - YouTube_
Subtle details mattered too. **Free samples**, tie-in merchandise, and physical stunts had outsized impact because everything felt tangible and freshly invented. There was no "keep scrolling" reflex blocking your message. Customers actually _engaged_ with a storefront banner like it was an invitation. That kind of trust is worth more than ten thousand paid impressions today.
texts.6:
## Unsurprising Yet Criminally Underrated: The 1990s Blueprint
Modern marketers steal from this era constantly, but rarely admit it. The nineties principles are dead simple: **make Americans feel something as they open their wallet**. Whether it was flag-paint-level patriotism or a $1 Happy Meal, the trick relied on emotional currency more than ad spend. That's a lesson most 2020s CMOs still absurdly overlook while chasing algorithm metrics.
So next time you skip a banner ad, remember: in 1996, a guy with a chicken bucket dressed as Uncle Sam got an _entire nation_ saluting. Those promotions looked crude by today's standards, yet they permanently reshaped how American households thought about brand identity. The 1990s didn't need a viral video — they needed a few buckets, a parade float, and sheer midsummer wanderlust. Mission accomplished, decades ago.
